topic: Why you hear your name in a noisy room
hook: Your brain is quietly listening for your name, even in a loud room.

blocks.narration: Your brain is quietly listening for your name, even in a loud room where you are ignoring every other conversation.
blocks.visual: A clay person at a crowded clay party, one ear softly glowing, colorful sound waves swirling around the room

blocks.narration: It is called the cocktail party effect. In a nineteen fifty-nine experiment, about a third of people caught their name in ignored speech.
blocks.visual: A clay person wearing big headphones, one ear cup dim and gray, the other side with a bright spark of light

blocks.narration: Your brain's attention filter never fully switches off; it just quietly decides what matters. Follow for one brain fact a day.
blocks.visual: A clay brain holding a small sieve that filters colorful sound droplets, letting one golden droplet through

cta: Follow for one brain fact a day.

captions.hook_line: Ever heard your name across a noisy room? That's your brain's filter at work 🧠
captions.body: Psychologists call it the cocktail party effect. In Neville Moray's 1959 experiment, about a third of people noticed their own name in a message they were told to ignore.
captions.share_line: Send this to the friend who always hears their name.

youtube_title: Why You Hear Your Name in a Crowd

sources.claim: Moray (1959), own name in the unattended message
